video_title: Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is Running Out of Copper
transcript: Welcome to Sourcery. The potential of photonics. The technology for connecting these GPUs . A platform for global payroll and HR. 8 billion operational data points. Scalable companies instead of startups. It's better to have a million of one thing than one of everything else. Building an intellectual layer for defense. There is a lack of capacity. Missing memory chips. We have reached the physical limit of what we can still do. Yannick and Gerwig, welcome to the annual Sourcery and Strikes gala. We are in Monaco and we will dive into the topic of photonics and what you are creating at Teema . But before we get to that, we'll have a long talk about photonics. So, Yannik, I would like to start with your experience, and then, Herwig, we will move on to yours. How did you get into photonics? I was one of those nerdy kids who would sit in their bedroom all day playing with LEGOs. So it's natural that I went to engineering school 20 years ago, and back then silicon photonics was a nascent niche industry with no job prospects. So I decided to jump on this train. I did my PhD in this field, and then had the opportunity to move to San Diego to join a startup that was trying to commercialize silicon photonics—one of the first companies to do so . I returned to IMEC, where I worked for a while on laser integration for silicon photonics, and 5 years ago I joined Nvidia. Back then, I still had to explain to people what Nvidia was. We started from scratch. We have developed silicon photonics technology to the level of a finished product. And now I'm starting work at Teema. Rick, how did you get involved? I have been an investor for most of my life, and became an operator very late. But I focused on deep technologies for quite some time and almost ten years ago I entered the exciting world of photonics. I realized 3-4 years ago that the train was leaving and there were huge gaps in the supply chain, and that is what we are trying to solve at Teema, understanding that Yannicke's visionary choice 20 years ago to study silicon photonics was what made Belgium famous and created a broad and deep talent base. I have dedicated my entire life to finding, developing, and supporting talent, and I hope we can do the same here. So, let's outline the state of the market and the path of chip development to this point, why copper is becoming obsolete, and why the focus is now shifting to photonics and lasers. Um, could you explain that a little more, and also why Europe? I think the market was the part that really got me into it. We saw much greater opportunities than what most people in this industry saw. This happened because we spoke to data center CTOs and understood what their need really was and how photonics could help solve it. We listened very carefully to some of the gurus in our ecosystem, like Andy Bechtolsheim, calling out numbers that far exceeded the forecasts of even the most optimistic analysts, and we felt that they were very well informed, and that's what pushed us to do this. And, to answer your question about where we are today. So, if you think about AI, you think about GPUs, right? You think about these computing systems that actually run the models. But models have become so large that they no longer fit on a single GPU . Therefore, we need to connect many GPUs together to run these models. Traditionally, copper connections were used for this, but as these processors get faster, they need more data, more data at a higher speed, and copper is gradually exhausting its resources. That's why we're moving to optical connections, which provide significantly higher bandwidth for data transmission. So, yeah, right here... I recently interviewed Tony Kim from BlackRock in Paris at the Raise AI Summit, and we were analyzing the entire industry. He says a massive $10 trillion restructuring is underway. One of the most affected and critical places for such costs is data centers, as today's legacy data center infrastructure is not built for AI and is completely inefficient. They consume a lot of water, a lot of energy, and the chips used there are simply outdated and cannot cope with the parametric models available on the market. So I would like to get a better understanding from some of you about the difference in the architecture of those data centers and how they are transforming with this new construction. This is probably a question for you. Yes. So, if you compare a traditional hyperscale data center to a modern AI factory, one of the big differences is that there is significantly more traffic between different servers. If you think back to a traditional Google search five years ago, your traffic was actually directed to a single computer that found the answer and sent it back. Now, if you think about modern AI infrastructure, as I said, models no longer fit on a single GPU, so there's already a connection between GPUs. But now, in the era of agent-based AI, the model makes a call to a specific tool located on another server, which returns the results back to the GPU. So, there is a lot of traffic in the data center that is very sensitive to delays. In fact, it's the time in between when all these different calculations can be performed. So, what this really means is that you need a much flatter network. Instead of a very deep hierarchical tree of switches, you need a much flatter network. This means many more direct connections between switches and GPUs. So, essentially, a much denser network than what was in traditional hyperscale systems. If you ask a data center CTO: “What keeps you up at night?” Energy consumption is the number one answer because it is a matter of their survival. They don't know how to solve it. Their CEO says, "We have to grow. " "We have to grow." And he replies: " Okay, but where?" Because no one can provide the power grid. Google spent three years negotiating with Amsterdam and was eventually forced to move its plans to Belgium because they simply couldn't get access to the power grid. And so , given their ambitious growth plans, it requires a much more fundamental solution that can scale to the size of the problem, right? So, there are many data centers, and even more are planned. Therefore, network modernization or construction of new power plants cannot take place in the time required . And here, you know, every paradigm shift in deep technology needs a killer app. For photonics, which has been developed for over 20 or even 30 years from the scientific side, the energy consumption of data centers in the field of AI is the same killer application. And so we got to where we are today : it's great, but no one was prepared for this speed of change. The pace of change came on November 22, with the release of ChatGPT. It went viral like nothing before. And with this growth came the realization: okay, we need to move to photonics. Nvidia has taken the lead in this. They have been talking about photonics for a long time , but finally said: it's time to act. In the 24th, they talked about it even louder. In '25, they really pushed the market. In the 26th, they showed the market what they meant by their investments in Lumentum and Coherent. In the first 6 months of this year, they invested four times more than the total market volume. And now everyone understands: oh, the supply chain is not ready for this . Innovations are ready. Photonics scientists and developers have done a tremendous amount of work, but it needs to be traced back to the very beginning: from raw materials, tools, and to the production infrastructure. I think that's where the problem lies today, and that's part of what we're trying to solve . How many photonic companies are there now? I interviewed Lumentum CEO Michael Herleston, and even just looking at this company, you can see that they are overwhelmed with demand. Their shares increased a thousandfold in a year. This is madness. And he only came there a year and a half ago. So he actually ended up in his place at the right time. I'm curious what the market situation looks like for existing companies and how it all works together? I believe that, again , we need to understand the scale of change in this market. For years, photonics was an academic field with limited applications, for which the supply chain was ready at the appropriate scale. And now suddenly Nvidia comes along and says, "No, no, guys , this is much, much bigger." And, of course, Lumentum and Coherent are two leading companies in the West that do this. They are the only ones who have such great power. If you look at the rest of the industry, let's say the traditional players like TSMC, Global Foundries, Tower, they have made a huge effort, investing in what fits into their supply chain, in their manufacturing process, namely, in the manufacture of silicon photonics wafers. But if you deliver an Nvidia plate, it's not at all what they ordered. They ordered a ready-made chip. So, much more is needed. First of all, lasers produced by Lumentum and other companies. And this should scale significantly. This is difficult because the bandwidth of the equipment is not at all what is needed. The efficiency and yield of the finished product do not meet standards. And as for the substrates, the raw materials are really in short supply. There are only a handful of suppliers on the market. And on top of all these problems, we now have the split between East and West, which is becoming quite problematic. So, in all of this, we believe that Europe is in an advantageous position. Because industrial capacity and infrastructure were available in Europe. This is what we purchased. There are photonics specialists there who have been trained for decades. There was industrial human resource potential there, which was released after the closure of large factories. The combination of all this, together with the desire for European sovereignty, puts us in the perfect position to do this from Europe. So let's get to the founding of the company and how you all came together. How did this process go? Yes. We were developing the concept of specialized photonic manufacturing on a much larger scale. We looked around . We have seen that all the big players are only involved in the initial stage of the process, as I said, silicon wafers. We have seen a lot of innovation, but mostly at the level of university startups. So there was actually no industrial player in the middle. And when we were making plans for 2023-24 , we probably got a little lucky, because a large European plant went bankrupt. So we took the opportunity and grabbed it . We just bought it. And this provided, in my opinion , a great combination: firstly, 20 kilometers from IMEC, a leading world research center; many talents, secondly, many industrial talents; as I said, infrastructure that was ready to go just when everyone needed it. Because when you want to build a foundry of this size, it's a 3-5 year project. This includes obtaining permits, licenses, and building the entire complex—it's not just clean rooms, the infrastructure is quite complex. So the fact that all of this was ready to launch in 2024 was, you know, a lucky coincidence, I would call it, and that's why we immediately went for it, starting to talk to both parties at the same time. When I say “both sides,” I mean we started talking to industrial and photonics talent and said, look. Europe has successfully invested in photonic innovations for 20-30 years . So, to answer your question, our schedule is to start production next year, in 2027, and we are working towards full capacity by 2028. So our deadlines are tight.
